title: Multimodal CT-pathology imaging deep learning model for risk stratification in resected stage I lung adenocarcinoma
desc: Lung adenocarcinoma is a highly heterogeneous disease, highlighting the need for more accurate prognosis prediction. We developed a multimodal deep learning model combining preoperative computed tomography (CT) and postoperative whole slide image (WSI) to predict the disease-free survival (DFS) of resected stage I lung adenocarcinoma. Based on a cohort of 1078 patients from multiple centers, our dual-information instance neural network achieved superior performance over unimodal approaches. The risk stratification defined by the model effectively distinguished DFS in both validation cohorts and served as an independent predictor, suggesting the complementary value of the model beyond clinicopathological factors. An exploratory scoring system integrating the model-derived risk stratification with key clinicopathological factors was developed, identifying patients with significantly different prognostic outcomes. Further analyses suggested that patients with high-risk stage IB disease or high scores might derive DFS benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy, warranting prospective validation. Beyond its predictive capacity, the model also provided morphological insights, identifying prognostically significant structures such as tertiary lymphoid structures and stroma barriers, while RNA-sequencing analysis revealed distinct oncogenic pathway activation and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments in high-risk patients. By leveraging routinely acquired clinical images, this multimodal approach offers a practical tool for improving prognostic stratification, with potential implications for informing patient selection for adjuvant chemotherapy in resected stage I lung adenocarcinoma.

title: Deep learning-based CT segmentation of mandibular bone invasion in oral squamous cell carcinoma.
desc: [BMC oral health] Accurate identification of mandibular invasion by oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is important for virtual surgical planning, but manual delineation on CT is challenging and time-consuming. This retrospective proof-of-concept study evaluated automated segmentation of the mandible and radiologically apparent bone invasion and explored centerline-based assessment of longitudinal tumor extent for computer-aided design/computer-aided manufacturing (CAD/CAM) planning. Fifty preoperative CT examinations from 50 patients with histopathologically confirmed mandibular invasion were included. Thirty examinations were used for model development and 20 for independent testing. A three-dimensional MedNeXt architecture implemented within nnU-Net was trained applying expert-reviewed CT reference segmentations. Performance was assessed using Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), precision, recall, average symmetric surface distance and 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance. Spatial localization, longitudinal invasion-span differences and signed centerline-projected endpoint errors were assessed in the holdout cohort. Mean mandibular DSC was 0.965 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.961-0.969; median 0.967). Mean invasion DSC was 0.553 (95% CI, 0.425-0.660; median 0.623), with mean precision of 0.742 and recall of 0.483. Predicted invasion overlapped the CT reference in 18/20 examinations (90%); 16/20 (80%) achieved DSC ≥ 0.20. Two cases were completely missed. Among the 18 evaluable cases, the median absolute invasion-span difference was 7.01 mm (interquartile range, 5.08-13.00 mm) and the median symmetric endpoint distance was 5.88 mm (3.19-9.16 mm). The present proof-of-concept study demonstrates the technical feasibility of automated CT segmentation of the mandible and radiologically apparent mandibular invasion by OSCC. The approach may support transmission of radiological tumor extent into virtual resection planning. Larger multicenter studies and prospective clinical validation are needed to establish its impact on planning accuracy and workflow efficiency.

title: Moving Generality from Model to Modeler: LLM Agents for PHM on a Deployment-Style Benchmark
desc: Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) now help develop many models published as general solutions. Should generality instead reside in the agent that builds a model for each new task? We examine this question in prognostics and health management (PHM), where every model must work on unseen equipment. Our deployment-style benchmark, NextUnit-Bench, covers 24 public datasets split into 58 folds that hold out units or operating conditions; each agent has two hours to deliver an executable predictor, then run on the hidden units. First, frontier agents outperform AutoML, which reaches less than half the best agent's score, and faithful implementations of published methods on four datasets, of which only 6 of 30 beat the strongest agent's own design; published accuracies, where reproducible, rest on the papers' own conventions, and a single convention, capping the remaining life of test engines, can halve the reported error. Second, the agents' advantage is a design made on each machine's data; once made, a plain-text plan of a few hundred words carries most of the gap between two frontier agents, and given a weaker agent's plan, the strongest agent falls to that agent's level, often to identical predictions. Before touching the data, however, it matters little whose plan an agent carries out, and domain toolkits appear to help neither: what sets the strongest apart is how much it learns from the data. Third, such designs reach only implementers that can execute them: given the strongest agent's designs, a locally deployable open-weight model delivers half as often, even when they are lightened, and scores no higher than without them. Generality, we argue, is not disappearing but moving, from the model to the modeler.

title: Toward a digital twin of the ICU patient: Forecasting and treatment response in a generative event model
desc: A digital twin of a patient in intensive care would forecast the patient's course and what a treatment would change. Generative event models, trained to continue a patient's electronic health record (EHR), have been proposed as a path toward such twins. We trained TWICE, a 79M-parameter decoder-only transformer, on the ICU records of one academic health system (127,332 training patients and 1.57 billion tokens). We evaluated it on clinical prediction tasks, generation fidelity, individual trajectories and counterfactual validation. Reading 19 clinical outcomes off 50 simulated futures, with no task-specific training, TWICE matched the best of 144 supervised configurations on held-out patients (mean AUROC 0.836 vs. 0.834). It led on events that change care within a day and trailed on death. With the training data fixed, more and longer simulated futures were worth more than a 6.8-fold larger model. Its generated records matched real ones closely and were as specific to each patient as its own variability allowed. Its predicted risk rose as events approached. Pre-specified controls showed that it reproduced the side effects of drugs and was barely moved by an inert drug. On the values that treatments are given to correct, however, an opposite treatment moved its forecasts like the right one. TWICE forecasts ICU events about as well as task-specific models, and we see it as a step toward a digital twin of the ICU patient.

title: What Does an Agent-Run Clinic Cost? Protocol for a Prospective Observational Study of the Compute Cost of Completed Work in a Clinical Agent Fleet
desc: Background: Decisions about deploying large language model (LLM) agents in health care require the cost of completed work in production. Published evidence reports benchmark accuracy, benchmark-level cost, and time or financial outcomes for ambient documentation, and list prices alone do not determine the cost of completed work. To our knowledge, no deployed clinical agent fleet has published a measurement method that ties compute cost, latency, failures and retries to completed work. Objective: This study aims to estimate the compute cost of completed work by the orchestrated clinical agents of a deployed LLM agent fleet over a 12-week window of production telemetry, using estimators, data-quality gates and an analysis plan fixed before any window data are extracted for the study. Methods: The setting is a private outpatient clinic in London, United Kingdom, where wai, a multi-agent system supporting clinic operations, is deployed. The population is every run of the 20 orchestrated clinical documentation and decision-support agents starting between September 21 and December 13, 2026. The run store writes 2 records for every run, a non-terminal record before the model call and a terminal record after it, and has no attempt counter or parent-run link. Estimators defined on that structure cover cost per resolved execution and per completed intention, retry and failed-intention shares of compute, error and failure rates, latency, cost per draft offered for clinician review and a latency-cost frontier, by agent, task class and acceptance stratum. Cost is recorded in GBP pence, converted from provider-returned US dollar cost at a fixed rate and rounded per model call. The plan fixes weekly aggregation, small-cell suppression, bootstrap intervals over weeks, 2 prespecified comparisons, 5 sensitivity analyses and 4 data-quality gates whose failure converts an estimate into a bound or an unmeasured stratum. Two staff-level measures in an earlier version were dropped. Revenue, pricing, margin and staffing inference are excluded. Results: The measurement window opened on September 21, 2026, and closes on December 13, 2026, and telemetry is being recorded in routine operation. Aggregate whole-table counts that include window records were extracted on November 19, 2026, for companion manuscripts and are disclosed. title: Machine Learning-based Transcriptomic Data Analysis of Long COVID Patients: Generating Hypotheses for Molecular Signatures
desc: Introduction: Long COVID (LC) remains a global public-health challenge, affecting an estimated 10-30% of COVID-19-survivors. Machine learning (ML) can help identify molecular features associated with LC. Human ion channels (HICs), that regulate immune-cell signaling and cellular homeostasis, may contribute to LC-associated processes and offer insights into relevant pathways and potential drug-repurposing candidates. Methodology: RNA-seq data from COVID-19-recovered and LC patients across six datasets were integrated, preprocessed, and corrected for batch effects. Supervised ML models were evaluated using leave-one-batch-out validation, with SHAP identifying features across validation folds. Functional enrichment, host-host and host-viral protein-protein interaction analyses were performed, followed by drug interaction analysis of potential HICs within the resulting interactome. Results: A support vector classifier with an RBF kernel achieved a mean-AUC of 0.664 across six validation folds. SHAP analysis of the three selected folds (AUC = 0.722, 0.836, and 0.817) identified 225, 153, and 241 genes, respectively. Functional enrichment highlighted pathways including histidine metabolism and TNF signaling. Among the 613 genes identified across these folds, 9 were HICs and 39 were immune signaling-related genes (ISGs), whose protein-protein interaction analysis revealed a pharmacologically relevant interactome. Furthermore, four HICs including CLCN3, KCNQ3, RYR1, and ZACN interacted with 30 approved drugs. Conclusion: ML-based analysis of integrated RNA-seq data identified HICs and ISGs associated with LC, while functional enrichment and PPI analyses provided insights into their potential biological relevance. Drug interaction analysis further highlighted candidate HIC-targeting drugs for future investigation in LC management. This computational framework provides preliminary, hypothesis-generating insights to guide future research.

Artificial intelligence model for pancreatic cancer risk prediction in patients with pancreatic cystic lesions
desc: Pancreatic cystic lesions (PCLs) are prevalent and potential precursors of pancreatic cancer. Cancer risk assessment is a crucial step in PCL management, but the complexity and limited accuracy of existing approaches contribute to suboptimal patient care. We developed and validated an artificial intelligence (AI) model that uses radiology reports and clinical data to predict the future risk of pancreatic cancer in patients with PCLs. The model was developed and tested in a 13-year retrospective cohort comprising 23,398 abdominal CT/MRI examination reports from 8707 patients with PCLs across a multisite healthcare system. Of these, 430 (1.8%) corresponded to patients who later developed pancreatic cancer, defined as adenocarcinoma, invasive mucinous neoplasm, or high-grade dysplasia. Among the models evaluated, XGBoost achieved the highest performance, with AUCs of 0.960, 0.945, and 0.944 for predicting pancreatic cancer incidence at 1, 3, and 5 years after imaging, respectively. The model outperformed guideline-based risk stratification, with AUC improvements of 0.161 to 0.235 (P < 0.001). For examinations conducted within a year before cancer diagnosis, radiologists identified potential cancer in 51.5% of cases, while the AI model flagged 82.3%. These findings support the potential of AI to complement existing approaches for individualized pancreatic cancer risk stratification in patients with PCLs.

title: Artificial intelligence and enhanced recovery after surgery: from protocol-driven pathways to adaptive perioperative care systems (cognitive ERAS).
desc: [Minerva anestesiologica] Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) programs have transformed perioperative care through standardized, evidence-based pathways, improving outcomes across surgical specialties. However, increasing patient complexity and heterogeneity expose important limitations of protocol-driven approaches, which often fail to capture dynamic physiological variability and individualized recovery trajectories. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a pathway to overcome these constraints by integrating longitudinal perioperative data and generating individualized risk predictions. However, prediction alone is insufficient for clinically meaningful personalization, which requires causal reasoning to estimate which interventions are most likely to improve outcomes for specific patients and at different stages of recovery. In this context, ERAS may evolve toward a data-informed, adaptive care system that integrates prediction, causal inference, and supervised workflow coordination. Emerging agentic AI systems may further extend ERAS beyond passive decision support toward structured care orchestration within defined clinical governance boundaries. This review examines how different AI methodologies, including supervised learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, natural language processing, generative models, and causal inference, can be aligned with ERAS objectives across the perioperative continuum. We also critically evaluate current evidence and key barriers to implementation. Looking forward, the convergence of AI, digital health technologies, and continuous patient monitoring may enable the emergence of cognitive ERAS, a data-driven perioperative care model that integrates prediction, causal estimation, and continuous learning to deliver personalized and dynamically adaptive recovery pathways.

title: Multi-Tier Edge Triage: Optimizing Latency for Safe Clinical Agents
desc: Deploying generative AI agents in enterprise clinical workflows requires enforcing multi-dimensional safety and compliance policies--preventing HIPAA Protected Health Information (PHI) exposure, maintaining clinical scope-of-practice boundaries, ensuring patient-appropriate reading comprehension, and preserving brand integrity--under interactive latency constraints. Synchronous outbound calls to cloud Large Language Model (LLM) judges add substantial network and decoding overhead onto the critical response path. We present Multi-Tier Edge Triage, a safety screening architecture that co-locates a compact Tier-1 sequence classifier on the clinical agent's host server, resolving clear queries in-process without a network round-trip and escalating only ambiguous queries to a Tier-2 cloud LLM judge. To evaluate Tier-1 encoders without length or unigram shortcuts, we construct four length-matched contrastive twin benchmarks seeded from MedSafetyBench, ASQ-PHI, and a synthetic four-mandate clinical assistant policy (Generic HealthCorp). While frozen local encoders match cloud models on structured PHI detection (>= 98.3% accuracy in 14x faster than cloud LLM evaluation on our benchmark host). Per-policy error analysis reveals ceiling local recall on PHI (100.0%), brand (100.0%), and clinical scope (98.7%-99.3%) violations, isolating residual errors to reading-level checks (93.3%-95.3%) and motivating targeted multi-tier escalation.

title: The unedited acceptance rate: a review-fidelity metric for human-in-the-loop clinical AI
desc: Objective. Guidance for large language model (LLM) drafting in clinical care relies on human review, yet review is rarely measured as a control. We aimed to define computable measures of review fidelity, establish which a deployed system can compute, and pre-specify their first analysis. Materials and Methods. For a multi-agent clinical system in routine use at one private London outpatient clinic, we defined acceptance coverage, attribution completeness, the unedited acceptance rate (UAR), a bounded normalized edit distance, availability latency and an unedited fast-approval rate (UFA). We checked each measure against the system's code and database structure at a fixed commit on four approval routes and pre-specified a prospective 12-week analysis. Results. The UAR equals the mass at zero of the edit-distance distribution, and availability latency bounds reading time from above only. Clinical documentation keeps draft and signed text with a recorded signer, so the core measures are computable there. Help-desk edit telemetry is written only when the agent's version has been stored. The WhatsApp agent route records no edit signal, and its approver need not be named. No route records when a draft is opened. Documentation accept events were not written before a change committed on November 16, 2026. Model-generated content, including live voice-agent speech, also reaches patients without approval. No measured values are reported. Discussion. Acceptance alone cannot separate accurate drafts from approval without reading, and three of four routes cannot yet support the family. Conclusion. Review fidelity can be specified as telemetry at the approval event. Validation against missed errors is required.

title: Deciphering state bridges via a single-cell large language model
desc: Large-scale single-cell transcriptomic data provide a new avenue for precision medicine by uncovering cellular heterogeneity. However, systematic comparison of remodeling patterns across various biological states remains unavailable. Here, we first developed a computational framework based on a foundation model of single cell biology, Universal Cell Embedding (UCE), to harmonize annotations comprising 36 cell types. Based on an integrated dataset of single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with 8,789 human samples comprising more than 59 million cells or nuclei across 614 biological states, we then embedded each state with a 36-dimensional vector in a unified space of cell-composition change and further deciphered states bridges by analyzing the relationships among the 614 state vectors. As a result, 22,161 significant bridges (P < 0.05) between the 614 states were revealed. Moreover, we successfully identified a number of well-known bridges such as bridge between Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease (P = 2.21e-15), suggesting the effectiveness of the proposed framework. More importantly, we uncovered a number of new bridges. Furthermore, analyses of the number of changed cell types (NCC) and Shannon entropy revealed heterogeneous and tissue-dependent patterns of cellular composition remodeling. This study provides a new strategy for identifying disease associations and potential therapeutic relationships by deciphering bridges between biological states from scRNA-seq landscape.

Health-state instability and progression in longitudinal clinical records reveal heterogeneous ageing trajectories
desc: Longitudinal clinical records capture health changes, but most models reduce them to endpoint risks or single-time biological-age estimates. We developed VitaFlux, a representation-learning framework that uses next-visit forecasting to encode clinical encounters as latent health states. Applied to 178,970 individuals with 4,439,390 aligned visits from the Zhejiang Population Health Cohort, VitaFlux learned a reproducible representation organized by age-associated, disease-burden and multisystem physiological variation. Forecast instability measured predicted health-state change at the next visit and was associated with observed one- and three-year mortality. Continuous trajectory measures captured heterogeneous progression, while current and forecast states improved the prediction of multiple clinical outcomes compared with a comprehensive clinical baseline. After cohort-specific adaptation, future-state forecasting outperformed a no-change persistence baseline in two independent aging cohorts. VitaFlux provides a unified framework for representing health-state position, forecasting near-term dynamics and quantifying longer-term progression from longitudinal clinical records.

title: AI foundation models for pathology and how to use them.
source: PubMed · Minimally invasive therapy & allied technologies : MITAT : official journal of the Society for Minimally Invasive Therapy
desc: [Minimally invasive therapy & allied technologies : MITAT : official journal of the Society for Minimally Invasive Therapy] Foundation models (FMs) are transforming artificial intelligence by generating large-scale representations of data that can be adapted across diverse downstream tasks. In computational pathology, the emergence of FMs trained on whole-slide images (WSIs) promises to reduce annotation burden, improve generalization, and enable multimodal disease modeling. This review summarizes the evolution in AI and deep learning that enabled pathology FM and surveys major publicly reported models developed by both academia and industry. To construct a comprehensive and representative survey of pathology foundation models, we performed a narrative literature search targeting peer-reviewed journals, preprint repositories (arXiv, medRxiv), and major Artificial Intelligence in medicine conferences up to mid-2026. The search strategy utilized combinations of keywords including 'pathology foundation model', 'self-supervised learning whole-slide images', and 'computational pathology vision transformers'. The survey highlights the current landscape of high-performing models while discussing their clinical promise alongside key technical and implementation challenges. Pathology foundation models represent a significant shift in the field. Future directions must focus on developing multimodal architectures and achieving seamless clinical integration to fully realize their potential.

title: Beyond Final Answers: Interpretable Tumor Immune Microenvironment Reasoning from H&E and mIF
desc: Readouts of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), such as CD8+ T-cell density, intra-epithelial infiltration and the Ki67 index, combine tissue architecture from H&E with cell phenotypes from multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF). Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) could automate these readouts with an explanation, but two gaps remain. Pathology MLLMs read H&E alone, while these readouts need the cell phenotypes that mIF measures. And their reasoning has no step-level truth to be checked against, so R1-style reinforcement learning rewards only the final answer and leaves the reasoning unverified. Same-section H&E and mIF provide what both gaps lack: mIF measures every cell without manual annotation, which gives cell-level ground truth for each step that clinical guidelines prescribe, from delineating a tissue compartment to counting and normalizing the marker-positive cells within it. We therefore present HERMES (H&E-mIF Reasoning with Multimodal Evidence Supervision), an R1-style MLLM that reasons jointly over paired H&E and mIF in guideline steps and is trained with a process reward that checks every stated quantity against this truth. Across four field-level TIME tasks in colorectal cancer, HERMES (4B) reaches an average accuracy of 84.5%, compared with 74.7% for the strongest of twelve proprietary, general, medical and pathology MLLMs, and a higher share of its intermediate quantities is correct than for the strongest open-weight baseline. Without the process reward, reinforcement learning barely improves on supervised fine-tuning (80.0% vs. 78.8%) and fewer stated quantities are correct; editing a decisive stated quantity changes the answer as implied in all 885 test questions. Without retraining, it keeps the highest average accuracy on an external cohort imaged with CODEX (76.4% vs. 67.3%) and on head and neck cancer, a cancer type absent from training (76.7% vs. 72.5%).

title: Interpretable competing-risk prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis from region-wide routine health data
desc: Background. Short-term prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in cirrhosis is complicated by the competing risk of death from liver disease. We aimed to develop an interpretable model on region-wide routine data that predicts HCC while separating competing mortality, and to compare it with established risk scores. Methods. From a region-wide cohort of adults with cirrhosis in the Andalusian Population Health Database, we trained the model on 17,177 patients with a prediction date set 12 months before their outcome, between 2020 and 2023. From one year of electronic health records before that date (demographics, liver and chronic disease codes, and eight routine laboratory tests), an Explainable Boosting Machine without interaction terms classified the following 12 months as HCC, death or liver transplantation without HCC, or event-free. We evaluated it in 20 repeats of 5-fold cross-validation against a binary model, a model with pair interactions and a model using the full health record, all on the same folds. We then applied the cross-validated models, without retraining, at the first routine encounter at which aMAP or the Toronto HCC Risk Index could be computed, and compared them with the scores in patients followed forward under competing risks, with and without a 6-month washout and with each province left out of training in turn. Findings. 771 patients (4.5%) developed HCC within 12 months and 3,314 (19.3%) died or underwent liver transplantation without HCC (3,061 deaths, 253 transplants). In cross-validation, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for HCC was 0.734 (SD 0.018). A binary formulation, pairwise interactions and the full health record (more than 3,000 features) did not improve it; the full record lowered it by 0.024. At routine encounters the model discriminated 12-month HCC better than aMAP (time-dependent AUC 0.790 vs 0.688; difference +0.102, 95% CI +0.071 to +0.132) and the Toronto HCC Risk Index (0.761 vs 0.703; +0.057, +0.032 to +0.081), and remained better after excluding HCC diagnosed within 6 months (concordance difference +0.055 and +0.040) and when each of the eight provinces was left out of training. At equal group size, its high-risk group held as much HCC as the scores' high-risk categories, with 20-28% fewer competing deaths. title: Machine learning prediction of antimicrobial resistance in respiratory metagenomes
desc: Background: Targeted therapy for patients with suspected respiratory infections traditionally requires bacterial culture followed by phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), a process that can take up to 5 days. In acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), delays in identifying the causative pathogen and its resistance profile may be especially harmful because patients are critically ill and often receive broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics. The growing burden of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) further complicates clinical decision-making by reducing effective treatment options and increasing the risk of inadequate initial therapy. Culture-free, AI-driven computational metagenomic strategies have the potential to drastically shorten this window, enabling more rapid targeted therapy prescription. To show the feasibility of such approaches, we develop a proof-of-concept framework based on clinical metagenomics. Methods: We simulated respiratory metagenomes using real-world bacterial genomes with associated antimicrobial susceptibility phenotypes. Each simulated metagenome contained a fixed commensal background and one clinically important respiratory pathogen, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or Pseudomonas aeruginosa, at 5% or 10% bacterial read abundance. Realistic reads were simulated for Oxford Nanopore, PacBio, and Illumina sequencing platforms. Random Forest (RF) classifiers were trained and evaluated using five-fold, strain-grouped cross-validation with fold-specific {chi}2-ranked 13-mer features. ResFinder and KARGA were included as reference-based metagenomics benchmarks and evaluated using the same five held-out folds across the three sequencing platforms and two pathogen-abundance conditions. Results: RF performance varied substantially across species, antibiotics, and sequencing platforms. The strongest and most consistent results were observed for K. pneumoniae, with accuracy reaching approximately 0.96 for ceftazidime, 0.93 for amikacin, and 0.92 for ciprofloxacin. Computational Drug Discovery in the Pandemic Era: AI-Enhanced Virtual Screening Approaches and Medical Informatics.
desc: [Healthcare informatics research] This narrative review examines how artificial intelligence-enhanced virtual screening (AI-VS), including multitarget screening strategies and hybrid AI-docking workflows, and the integration of medical informatics advance antiviral drug discovery and pandemic preparedness. We reviewed recent studies that used graph neural networks to predict binding affinity, molecular dynamics simulations to validate binding stability, absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) profiling frameworks, and protein structure prediction tools, including AlphaFold2 (2021) and AlphaFold3 (2024). A nonsystematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar identified seven representative studies published between 2020 and 2026, which were selected for their relevance, methodological innovation, and clinical applicability. Molecular dynamics simulations validated binding stability, while multi-target screening identified natural product inhibitors with favorable ADMET profiles. The hybrid AI-docking platform outperformed traditional docking, with VirtuDockDL achieving 99% accuracy and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.99 on benchmark datasets, although external validation across protein families remains limited. These values apply to the benchmark dataset used and should not be generalized to other protein families, antiviral targets, or real-world drug discovery settings. AI-VS has the potential to shorten computational screening timelines from years to weeks and provide scalable frameworks that may support pandemic preparedness; this acceleration concerns in silico screening, not the full experimental or clinical development process. These methods illustrate how computational-first approaches can accelerate early therapeutic discovery, although they did not directly lead to the approval of nirmatrelvir or molnupiravir. Future priorities include expanding chemical probe libraries, improving the precision of scoring functions, and integrating AI-VS with medical informatics infrastructure.

title: Communication-Efficient Federated Learning of Latent Patient Representations from Multi-Institutional EHRs
desc: Electronic health records (EHRs) contain rich health information for uncovering latent patient representations and clinically meaningful subgroups. Learning from EHR data across institutions is valuable because representations learned at a single site may reflect local data patterns and lack generalizability, yet pooling patient-level records across institutions is often impractical because of privacy constraints and communication costs. We propose a communication-efficient, non-iterative federated spectral method for learning shared latent representation components from multi-institutional EHRs, in which each institution shares aggregate marginal frequencies and a low-rank spectral summary while keeping patient-level records local. A central server aggregates these summaries with the pooled marginal frequencies to recover both the shared low-rank structure and the canonical row-normalization direction required for interpretable representation recovery. We prove row-wise recovery guarantees and error bounds, with a leading federated variance term matching a corresponding lower bound under explicit regularity conditions. Simulations show that our method closely matches pooled analysis in estimating latent representation components, improves as more sites contribute summaries, and outperforms single-site and existing federated benchmarks across a range of data settings. Applied to real-world multi-facility EHR data for stroke patients, the method learns interpretable patient representations that highlight clinically distinct subgroups and could help inform subgroup-specific care.

title: Asking Conversational Artificial Intelligence about Health and Subsequent Actions among Adults in Japan: A Cross-sectional Web Survey
desc: Introduction: People increasingly ask conversational artificial intelligence (AI) about health; however, how this relates to care seeking in Japan, where universal health coverage renders care accessible, remains unknown. This study described how many adults ask AI about health, why and when, what they do afterward, and how much they trust AI compared with other sources. Methods: This two-stage cross-sectional survey employed a commercial web panel (October-November 2026). A screening survey of adults aged [≥]20 years (10,000 responses; 8,209 analyzed) estimated prevalence. A main survey of users (1,000 responses; 735 analyzed) asked about purposes, the most recent use and subsequent actions, and trust in seven information sources. Responses were weighted by sex and age. Results: In the past 6 months, 40.3% of adults (95% confidence interval, 39.3-41.4) asked conversational AI about health. The most recent use occurred before a medical visit for 39.0%, after a visit for 23.4%, and when no visit was being considered for 37.6%. Subsequently, 35.4% visited a medical facility; 12.8% (10.3-15.3) decided not to visit or postponed a visit (5.1% of all adults). Forgoing or delaying was more frequent among users with high trust in AI (trusting it completely or a lot; 22.5% vs. 10.9% among others). Among pre-visit users, it was less frequent with high trust in health professionals (16.7% vs. 30.9%) and did not clearly differ by trust in AI. Of users, 61.4% had high trust in health professionals and 14.3% in AI. Conclusions: In Japan, approximately 4 in 10 adults asked AI about health, and 1 in 8 users forwent or delayed a visit. This was more common with high trust in AI; among pre-visit users, it was associated with low trust in health professionals. How trust in AI and health professionals relates to care seeking warrants further study.

title: Integrating CRISPRi perturbation responses and transcription-factor binding priors for regulatory network inference in triple-negative breast cancer
desc: Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) represents an aggressive breast cancer subtype that lacks actionable cell-surface receptors, restricting frontline systemic management to cytotoxic chemotherapy. While recent functional epigenomics shows that TNBC progression is governed by non-coding regulatory remodeling at distal super-enhancers, conventional Gene Regulatory Network (GRN) inference methods rely on observational transcriptomic co-expression, which suffers from technical dropouts and confounding correlations that inflate false discoveries (>30%). Here, we present an interventional network inference framework that integrates large-scale single-cell CRISPR-interference perturbation sequencing (Perturb-seq; GSE224986, 95,678 cells across 11,975 sgRNAs) with ENCODE Factorbook ChIP-seq physical transcription factor binding priors across 819 somatic mutation-associated enhancer loci in human TNBC (MDA-MB-231). Our pipeline reconstructed a tripartite network yielding 5,935 physical TF-enhancer edges, 383,757 functional enhancer-gene edges, and 542,760 unique TF-target gene functional pairs across 372 active enhancers. Topological centrality prioritized master transcriptional drivers governing TNBC oncogenic signaling, including CTCF, POLR2A, EP300, JUND, MYC, and FOS, which regulate Hallmark programs for Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (p = 1.2 x 10-9) and cell cycle progression. Explainable machine learning (SHAP TreeExplainer) revealed non-linear, thresholded transactivation dynamics for AP-1 and MYC. Quantitative benchmarking against held-out CRISPRi ground truth demonstrated strong discriminatory accuracy (AUROC = 0.8999, AUPRC = 0.8745, Precision = 90.13%, FDR = 9.87%), substantially outperforming GENIE3 (AUPRC = 0.6323, FDR = 35.73%) and co-expression correlation (AUPRC = 0.6814). In silico-simulated driver feature silencing correlated with experimental responses (R2 = 0.473, p < 10-122), and master driver signatures significantly stratified overall survival in the METABRIC (n = 320) and TCGA-BRCA (n = 160; p [≤] 0.019) cohorts. Finally, in silico perturbation modeling indicated that multi-target epigenetic combinations achieved 93% topological disruption of oncogenic regulatory connectivity, nominating prioritized candidate circuits for experimental validation.

Targeting protein degradation strategies in drug discovery: integrating PROTACs, ubiquitination biology, and AI-driven design.
desc: [Molecular biomedicine] Targeted protein degradation (TPD) has emerged as a transformative therapeutic strategy for eliminating disease-associated proteins, including targets that remain challenging to modulate using conventional occupancy-driven inhibitors. Among TPD approaches, proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) exploit the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) to induce selective and event-driven degradation of proteins of interest (POIs). Despite rapid advances in PROTAC development, successful translation depends on interconnected determinants, including target degradability, ubiquitin ligase (E3) recruitment, warhead and linker properties, ternary-complex formation, ubiquitination efficiency, intracellular exposure, and pharmacokinetic behavior. This review provides an integrated, mechanism-oriented analysis of these determinants by linking PROTAC design, ubiquitination biology, computational approaches, and clinical development. We examine key principles governing PROTAC-mediated degradation, with emphasis on E3-ligase selection, linker design, ternary-complex geometry and cooperativity, ubiquitin (Ub)-acceptor lysine (Lys) accessibility, ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme (E2)/E3 context, proteasomal engagement, inefficient degradation, and the hook effect. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning for degradation-activity prediction, E3-ligase/POI pairing, ligand and linker optimization, ternary-complex modeling, and absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) assessment are critically evaluated alongside their technical and translational limitations. Preclinical developments, clinical-stage degraders, emerging TPD modalities, and major barriers to translation are also discussed. We propose an integrated framework linking distinct target ubiquitination patterns, degrader design, ternary-complex geometry, AI-enabled prediction, and pharmacokinetic/clinical constraints, providing a mechanism-informed roadmap for the rational development of next-generation protein degraders and identifying mechanistic bottlenecks and translational priorities across therapeutic settings.

title: MedicalRSI: Medical Recursive Self-Improving Agents via Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution
desc: Medical agents built on large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet most stay fixed once deployed and do not keep using their experience to improve later attempts. As a result, the same kind of error can recur across patients. To address this, existing self-improvement methods update an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) instead improves both the agent and its improving strategy. However, achieving RSI for medical agents is challenging, because clinical workflows rarely come with a reference harness, and a change that fixes early errors may not fix the problems the agent meets later. We propose MedicalRSI, an RSI framework built on Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution, in which one model plays two roles. The Solver is the medical agent itself, and the Improver is its learnable improving strategy, which writes a medical harness from the agent's failures. Each harness is rewarded by its gain over acting without it, and both roles are trained together, so the Improver keeps adapting to the problems the Solver has not yet solved. On multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, MedicalRSI outperforms existing context-level and weight-level self-improvement methods and transfers well to unseen workflows, new LLMs and new databases, a step toward medical agents that keep improving.

title: Task-specific fine-tuning versus frontier large language models for RoB 2 risk of bias assessment: development and external benchmark evaluation of RoB-BERT
desc: Background: Researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to assess risk of bias in randomized trials, but how task-specific fine-tuned models compare with frontier models remains uncertain. Objective: To develop RoB-BERT, a fine-tuned RoB 2 assessment system, and to compare its agreement with human assessments against that of three frontier LLMs. Methods: RoB 2 rates five bias domains and the trial overall as low risk, some concerns or high risk, based on answers to 22 signalling questions. RoB-BERT answers each question, quotes the supporting sentences from the trial report, and applies the official RoB 2 algorithm. We trained RoB-BERT on 5,304 reviewer-checked assessments, none from a test trial, and compared it with Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Argon, each given identical prompts and text, against 419 published human assessments (ROBoto2, LogiMed-RoB and Cochrane reviews) made without AI assistance. Each reference was the single published judgement for that trial, made by one assessor or agreed by two, rather than an expert reference standard, so we also report agreement between two human assessors of the same trial. Results: In ROBoto2, pairs of human assessors who rated the same trial agreed on 61.2% to 64.7% of domain judgements ({kappa} 0.15 to 0.35) and 46.2% to 50.0% of overall judgements ({kappa} 0.15 to 0.17); across the 185 ROBoto2 trials, RoB-BERT agreed with the human judgement on 67.4% ({kappa} 0.35) and 53.5% ({kappa} 0.20). Across all 419 assessments, domain agreement was 67.9% ({kappa} 0.29) for RoB-BERT, 65.0% ({kappa} 0.24) for Claude Fable 5.1, 52.7% ({kappa} 0.21) for GPT-6 Astra and 66.7% ({kappa} 0.26) for Gemini 4 Argon; overall agreement was 46.1% ({kappa} 0.16), 47.3% ({kappa} 0.17), 31.0% ({kappa} 0.03) and 46.5% ({kappa} 0.14), respectively. For domains the reference rated high risk, sensitivity was 22.2% for RoB-BERT, 23.1% for Claude Fable 5.1, 41.9% for GPT-6 Astra and 24.8% for Gemini 4 Argon, with specificity of 92.5%, 92.8%, 80.0% and 95.0%. On the 52 ROBoto2 trials rated by two assessors, the second assessor's sensitivity for the reference assessor's high-risk domains was 23.1% (specificity 90.3%) and RoB-BERT's was 30.8% (specificity 92.7%). RoB-BERT located 95.7% of its quotations verbatim in the report and cost US$0.005 per trial, 2% to 6% of the frontier models' cost. title: How predictable is an individual's DNA methylation?
desc: DNA methylation is largely shared among individuals of the same cell type, yet at specific genomic sites it differs substantially between individuals. Methods that predict methylation are usually evaluated by their accuracy over all sites. Because methylation at most sites is shared, this accuracy cannot show whether a method predicts an individual's methylation where individuals differ. We present individual-level methylation prediction at sites where individuals differ as a new challenge. Given the reference genome sequence, the methylation of other individuals of the same cell type, and measurements at some sites of a target individual, but not the individual's genotype, the task is to predict the target individual's methylation class (unmethylated, intermediate, or methylated) at the remaining sites. We evaluate predictions separately at sites with low and high variation across individuals. We compare four approaches: the average of other individuals, a sequence model (the DNA language model Nucleotide Transformer) fine-tuned on other individuals' methylation, the same model further fine-tuned on the target individual's measurements, and a local class-average approach using the target individual's nearby training-site class labels. Across 32 individuals from six human cell types, the average of other individuals matched or slightly exceeded both sequence models at sites with low variation among individuals. At the most variable sites, the average of other individuals performed worse than a random predictor that assigns classes at the observed class frequencies, whereas both sequence models performed substantially better than the average. Both sequence models also achieved higher mean weighted F1 than the local class-average approach. Fine-tuning on the target individual's measurements improved predictions more inside regions where other individuals show bimodal methylation (a mix of methylated and unmethylated DNA molecules within one sample) than outside them. Among the most variable sites, it also improved predictions at CpG islands for 25 of the 32 individuals. We conclude that individual-level methylation prediction is a distinct problem that is particularly challenging at sites where individuals differ, and that the benefit of an individual's own measurements is concentrated in genomic contexts identifiable from other individuals' methylation and genomic annotations.

desc: [Perspectives on medical education] Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming clinical practice, yet its integration into medical education remains largely unstructured. In China, where AI adoption is accelerating, little is known about how medical students perceive AI's role or what guidance they expect from educators. This study explores Chinese medical students' perspectives on AI in clinical training and their preferences for faculty engagement. Using educational cultural hegemony as a theoretical framework, the research team conducted in-depth, semi-structured interviews with 13 medical students across all five years of training at a medical school in China. Interviews addressed three sensitizing scenarios involving AI for clinical documentation, diagnostic assistance, and learning support. Transcripts were analyzed using Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes were identified: Learning in the Shadows describes how students use AI covertly due to uncertain policies; Trust but Verify captures students' nuanced stance on AI reliability; The Human Element reveals concerns that AI may erode clinical reasoning and patient-physician relationships within China's high-volume healthcare system; and Educator as Compass describes students' desire for faculty who proactively teach AI literacy and model appropriate use. Chinese medical students navigate AI use without formal guidance in an ambiguous space between enthusiasm and caution. They seek educators who acknowledge AI's presence and preserve humanistic medicine. Findings underscore the urgent need for curricular integration of AI literacy and faculty development, particularly within hierarchical educational contexts. These findings carry implications beyond China's borders, suggesting that when institutions fail to acknowledge emerging technologies, students adapt independently but not necessarily safely or equitably.

title: A High-Compression Transformer VAE for Efficient and Controllable 3D Medical Image Generation with Diffusion Transformers
desc: Many medical image processing tasks, such as completing missing regions or correcting acquisition artifacts, can be cast as volumetric generation conditioned on observations of the same patient. Diffusion Transformers offer scalable capacity and flexible conditioning for this setting, but they operate on a learned image representation that must preserve fine anatomical and pathological detail while keeping complete three-dimensional volumes tractable. We bring Transformer variational autoencoding and multimodal diffusion together to address this challenge. Trained on BrainTumor-256K, a 249M Transformer VAE encodes and decodes $256^3$ volumes 7.6x faster than a comparably sized CNN trained on the same collection. Their PSNR difference is near zero with training-sized crop inputs, but the Transformer leads by 0.749 dB with full-volume inputs and an unchanged scoring region. Increasing Transformer capacity to 499M improves PSNR across all four brain MRI evaluation sets while retaining 3.8x lower encoding-decoding latency than the CNN. Fast encoding also allows conditions to be constructed dynamically in image space during latent diffusion training. Within the compressed representation, a shared Diffusion Transformer integrates text and spatial references for volumetric synthesis, completion and restoration. The brain-trained autoencoder further transfers to non-brain MRI and CT without target-domain fine-tuning, extending its use beyond the anatomy and modality on which it was learned. The framework provides a reusable representation and conditioning interface for efficient, controllable medical image generation. Code is available at https://github.com/OncoMMAI/brainmri-vit-vae3d.

title: Unified Machine Learning Model for Early Detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment, Frailty, and Fall Risk Using Multimodal Motor-Function Data
desc: Background: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI), frailty, and fall risk often co-occur in older adults and share motor signs, yet they are screened and modeled separately. A unified model that predicts all 3 conditions from 1 sensor-based assessment could support earlier and more efficient screening, but such a model has rarely been developed or rigorously compared with separate models. Objective: This study aimed to develop a unified machine learning model that predicts MCI, frailty, and fall risk together from sensor-based motor-function data, compare it with separate single-label models, explain its predictions, and test its robustness. Methods: Community-dwelling older adults (n=79) completed a multimodal motor-function assessment with the Mizzou Point-of-Care Assessment System (MPASS), covering gait, sit-to-stand, static balance, step-down, and reaction time, with some tasks repeated under a dual-task condition. With demographic and family-history data, this yielded 59 features. Unified classifier-chain and single-label models were built with 5 algorithms across 6 modeling stages, evaluated with repeated nested cross-validation, and compared using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and paired bootstrap tests. The final model was explained with Shapley additive explanations (SHAP), and its robustness and the sufficiency of the sample size were tested with chain-input, chain-order sensitivity, domain-ablation, learning-curve, and power analyses. Results: With class weighting, the unified model had a higher mean AUC than the single-label models in 17 of 20 configurations and was never significantly worse, and it performed at least as well under nested model selection (0.615 vs 0.605; P=.58). The model overestimated risk for all 3 outcomes, most for frailty. Most features (43/59, 73%), led by stride length, were shared across the 3 conditions, with consistent SHAP rankings in training and test participants ({rho}=0.99). Predicted frailty was the most important input for fall risk, and the 45 sensor features alone performed as well as the full model. title: A2Holo: Dual-Stream Flow Matching of 3D Structure and a Protein Language Model for Conformational Transition Prediction
desc: Modelling a ligand-bound holo conformation from a ligand-free apo conformation is essential in structure-based drug discovery. We present A2Holo, which casts apo-to-holo prediction as flow matching between two experimental structures rather than generation from noise. It transplants the dual-stream joint attention of in-context image generation to residue-aligned protein language model embeddings and structure. Without ligand conditioning or stochastic sampling, A2Holo's single deterministic trajectory reaches a median C RMSD of 0.809 [A] on the D3PM benchmark, the lowest among existing methods. Its TM-score exceeds even the best of 10 samples from every stochastic baseline on at least 144 of 150 pairs. Beyond performance, we directly measure the transplanted multimodal mechanism itself. Because sequence and structure are residue-aligned, its joint attention can be measured at residue resolution and tested for reproducibility across independently trained model variants. Within the structure stream, the attention a residue receives recovers moving residues better than the attention it emits, and this asymmetry is learned. A2Holo demonstrates a successful multimodal transplant from in-context image generation to protein conformational change, with strong deterministic apo-to-holo prediction. It also provides a quantitative account of how that mechanism organises residue-aligned sequence and structure around the residues that move.

The arc of uncertainty across clinicians' interactions with AI.
desc: [Discover artificial intelligence] Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used in various clinical settings to support clinical reasoning and decision-making. Although they have demonstrated strong performance on medical knowledge and reasoning tasks, and early studies suggest potential to reduce medical errors, emerging evidence also highlights important safety concerns, including clinically significant management errors in outputs that may not be readily apparent to users. How these tools can be integrated into clinical practice to consistently lead to improved patient outcomes remains an open question. AI-assisted reasoning unfolds across a sequence of decisions: whether to use AI for the clinical question, how to engage with the tool, how to interpret its output, and whether to act. Each stage in this sequence introduces distinct risks, including inappropriate tool selection, incomplete or biased inputs, overconfidence in fluent responses, and failure to recognize error or appreciate nuance. These risks are further shaped by the same clinician factors that generally affect clinical reasoning such as experience, workload, and uncertainty management. Viewing the AI-clinician interaction as a process rather than a single moment highlights several key points of vulnerability but also opportunities for training. Ultimately, the safe use of AI may depend less on the quality of the model and more on the clinician's ability to recognize when its outputs should be questioned, verified, or set aside.

title: Feasibility of Multifrequency Neural Network-Based Wave Inversion in Ultrasound Time-Harmonic Elastography
desc: Ultrasound time-harmonic elastography (THE) is a non-invasive imaging technique that measures soft-tissue stiffness. Relying on the same principle of time-harmonic shear wave excitation as established magnetic resonance elastography (MRE), THE offers full field-of-view stiffness mapping at short acquisition times and sub-second temporal resolution across organs. However, reconstruction of shear wave speed maps from acquired tissue wavefields remains challenging due to speckle noise and sparse spatial coverage of the lateral component. Deep learning methods have shown promising results for image reconstruction in transient-based ultrasound elastography modalities but remain unexplored in THE. In MRE, MF-ElastoNet, a 2D multifrequency neural network-based wave reconstruction method trained on synthetic physics-based wave data, has shown high generalizability across dynamic ranges and resolutions. We investigated the potential of a multifrequency neural network-based wave inversion for THE, by performing a first feasibility analysis. To this end, we adapted the processing pipeline of MF-ElastoNet from MRE to THE. We tested our approach on THE acquired phantom data from the algorithms for mapping elastic modulus Challenge, as well as on in vivo liver THE in 4 healthy volunteers and 14 patients with focal liver lesions, including benign focal nodular hyperplasia, and malignant hepatocellular carcinoma and adenocarcinoma. MF-ElastoNet was successfully adapted to THE with in vivo liver testing. Compared with k-MDEV, the state-of-the-art wave inversion method for THE, Bland-Altman analysis showed a mean bias of -0.02 m/s (95% limits of agreement: -0.36 to 0.33 m/s).

title: Germline Variant Profiling of NA12878 Chromosome 22 Identifies the Loss-of-Function CYP2D6*3 and *4 Pharmacogenetic Alleles
desc: The approach used in this project to call germline variants from short-read sequencing data forms the basis of a great deal of current human genetics, whether it be in population studies or in diagnostic testing. A full germline variant-calling workflow according to the GATK Best Practices was constructed and carried out using public whole-genome sequencing data from the reference sample NA12878. In order to comply with the limitations of a laptop (an Intel Core i3, 8 GB of RAM, Ubuntu via WSL2), the analysis was limited to chromosome 22. The reads for chromosome 22 were streamed directly from the 1000 Genomes high-coverage CRAM file (run ERR3239334), converted into paired FASTQ files, checked using FastQC and MultiQC, and then cleaned with fastp. The cleaned reads were aligned to a GRCh38 reference containing only chromosome 22 using BWA-MEM, after which they were sorted, duplicates were marked and the base quality scores were recalibrated before variants were called with GATK HaplotypeCaller. The GATK-recommended hard filters were applied separately to SNPs and indels, and the variants that passed these filters were annotated using the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (VEP) and summarised with a Python script. From the 81,599 raw calls, 73,570 (90.2%) survived the filtering process, and the transition/transversion ratio for the SNPs that passed filtering was 2.04. Of the annotated variant alleles, 98.9% were already present in the catalogue, 734 affected the coding sequence in 270 genes, and no variant corresponded to a pathogenic entry in ClinVar. Examination using IGV verified the read support for the selected high-impact calls, including the variants that define the CYP2D6*3 and *4 alleles, consistent with the published genotype of NA12878. The main limitations were a reduced effective depth of 8.6x, resulting from an incomplete read-collation step which retained about 31% of the read pairs, and the use of a chromosome-only reference.

title: deeprok: highly accurate prokaryotic gene prediction through deep learning and overlap-aware decoding
desc: Prokaryotic gene prediction is often considered solved, yet widely used tools still disagree on many genes, chiefly short genes and translation starts. We present deeprok, an ab initio prokaryotic gene prediction method that combines a base-level neural network with an overlap-aware decoder, and refines start-site predictions with a self-trained neural ranker. On four curated genomes distant from its training data, deeprok made 10-18% fewer exact-match errors than Prodigal and GeneMarkS-2, and on 2,925 experimentally verified starts it made 21-41% fewer start errors. Furthermore, deeprok's base-level architecture reveals lineage-specific translation initiation signals. These results show that per-base deep learning combined with overlap-aware decoding can improve prokaryotic gene prediction, especially for resolving translation starts.

desc: [Academic medicine : journal of the Association of American Medical Colleges] The rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) by medical students has created two significant concerns: that students will use artificial intelligence (AI) for quick answers, short-circuiting the cognitive effort essential for deep learning, and that the satisfaction of discovery will be lost to algorithmic efficiency. This Scholarly Perspective reframes LLMs not as information retrieval systems, but as "Socratic Mirrors": interactive tutors grounded in established learning science (such as the desirable level of difficulty, social constructivism and zone of proximal development, the illusion of explanatory depth, and dual coding theory) that can restore the productive struggle that traditional LLMs often constrain. Drawing on the three functions of education framework, the authors argue that by handling qualification (the foundational work of content mastery), Socratic tutors free faculty to focus on what AI cannot provide: socialization (initiation into the norms and values of the profession) and subjectification (the formation of physicians as autonomous, ethical, and reflective practitioners). This potential is not merely theoretical. Empirical evidence from randomized controlled trials suggests that pedagogically engineered AI tutors, those designed to scaffold discovery rather than deliver answers, can significantly outperform traditional instruction. The studies demonstrate how LLMs configured as Socratic tutors can address the "2-Sigma" problem, offering personalized one-on-one tutoring at scale and moving medical education closer to the ideal of precision education. However, these studies are drawn from outside medical education, and the inferential leap to medical training, while theoretically grounded, remains empirically undemonstrated. The PICRAT (passive, interactive, creative, replacement, amplification, transformation) model is presented as a technology integration framework to ensure intentional rather than reactive AI integration. Together, these principles suggest a promising pathway toward scalable precision medical education that warrants formal evaluation in medical education contexts.

title: Surface Cues Over Structure: Probing LLM Behavior on Brain Connectivity Graphs
desc: Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) provides a noninvasive view of functional interactions across the brain, which can be represented as connectivity graphs for neurological disease analysis. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being paired with such representations, yet it remains unclear whether they genuinely reason over the underlying connectivity or simply respond to surface-level cues that may trigger learned priors. We probe this question through a controlled study of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) diagnosis from resting-state functional connectivity, isolating one factor at a time to determine what drives an LLM's predictions on brain connectivity graphs. Across six models, from small open-weight LLMs to a proprietary one, the same pattern holds: the results provide little evidence that predictions are consistently grounded in subject-specific connectivity. Brain region names, numeric formatting, and prompt framing shift what a model predicts without improving how well it separates ADHD subjects from Controls; perturbing the graph changes predictions no more for clinically meaningful regions than for random ones; and the models' own justifications contradict the values they cite, inconsistently interpreting the connectivity evidence provided to them. Across every probe, predictions follow the model's built-in class bias and the surface form of the prompt rather than the subject's connectivity, calling into question a premise underlying current LLM brain integration work. Our code is available at https://github.com/Roy025/ADHD-code.

title: Dependence-Aware Conformal Prediction for 3D Uncertainty Quantification in Molecular Docking
desc: Molecular docking plays a critical role in drug discovery by predicting three-dimensional (3D) binding poses of small molecules within proteins. However, docking predictions can contain substantial positional errors, making reliable uncertainty quantification essential. Conformal prediction (CP) provides a principled framework for uncertainty quantification, yet constructing compact 3D prediction regions with reliable joint coverage remains challenging due to heterogeneous atomic errors, dependence among spatial coordinates, and distribution shifts. We develop a dependence-aware CP framework for molecular docking that leverages a shared graph neural network (GNN) to estimate adaptive, asymmetric uncertainty intervals using local atomic and global molecular information. Copula-based joint calibration accounts for dependence among coordinate-wise nonconformity scores to construct compact 3D prediction boxes. We further introduce density ratio estimation (DRE) to adapt calibration under distribution shift. Experiments across three docking methods demonstrate that our approach reduces median prediction-box volumes by 37.40%, 95.00%, and 39.16% for AutoDock Vina, Protenix, and MedusaGraph, respectively, compared with a state-of-the-art CP baseline, while achieving empirical joint coverage close to the 90% target. Under the Molecular Group Split and controlled distribution shifts, DRE further reduces coverage deviations, highlighting the potential of dependence-aware and shift-adaptive calibration for reliable 3D molecular docking uncertainty quantification.

title: SonoAtlasWorld: Anatomy-Grounded Ultrasound World Models for Wide-Range Scanning
desc: Learning robotic ultrasound policies requires interactive environments for scalable data generation and repeatable evaluation, while exploration on real patients is limited by acquisition costs and safety constraints. Generative world models offer an alternative, but image history and probe actions alone do not ensure anatomical consistency across wide-range scans and changing acoustic windows. We introduce SonoAtlasWorld, an ultrasound world model built on anatomy as state. A persistent 3D anatomical asset extracted from computed tomography (CT) anchors each scan to a specific anatomy. Probe actions determine anatomical and acoustic visibility conditions for a causal ultrasound generator trained on clinical videos. Our three-stage pipeline combines anatomy-conditioned pretraining, causal conversion and long-rollout alignment. Inference optimizations achieve pose-to-ultrasound throughput of 81.2 FPS. To evaluate anatomical control beyond image similarity, we introduce the Action-Following Index (AFI), which measures normalized reconstruction gain over a static-prefix baseline. On 40 held-out 3D volumes, SonoAtlasWorld achieves liver and macro-organ AFI of 0.428 and 0.262, compared with at most 0.117 and 0.038 for the tested action- and geometry-conditioned methods. Long-rollout alignment reduces brightness drift by 3.46x at the end of 40 repeated scan cycles. SonoAtlasWorld also generates offline policy-training demonstrations and supports anatomically grounded closed-loop evaluation. Scaling the generated training data improves key-plane acquisition success from 48.2% to 81.2% on unseen anatomies in simulation, demonstrating its utility for robotic ultrasound policy learning.

title: Unsupervised tensor integration of hippocampal and colonic multi-omics reveals enteric neural signatures in cognitive aging
desc: Background: Molecular changes in peripheral tissues may provide insights into cognitive aging, but identifying relevant genes without using behavioral outcomes for feature selection remains challenging. Results: We applied tensor decomposition-based unsupervised feature extraction to publicly available hippocampal and colonic transcriptomic and promoter DNA methylation profiles from mice across five age groups. A tensor comprising tissue, molecular modality, age group, biological replicate, and gene dimensions was constructed using 16,080 shared genes. Higher-order singular value decomposition identified a component with a monotonic age pattern, shared tissue contributions, and opposing transcriptomic and methylation contributions. This component yielded 1,577 selected genes without using cognitive scores for feature selection. The corresponding colonic methylation score correlated with overall cognition (r=0.589; Benjamini--Hochberg-adjusted P=9.87 x10-7), although no significant associations remained after age adjustment. The selected genes were enriched for enteric neuronal and glial markers derived from a published single-cell atlas, with 5.10-fold and 4.65-fold enrichment, respectively. Comparison with the broadest available Boruta-selected gene set identified only 64 overlapping genes, leaving 1,513 genes selected exclusively by the tensor approach in this comparison. These remaining genes retained significant enrichment for synaptic processes and enteric neuronal and glial signatures using library-specific backgrounds. Conclusions: Unsupervised tensor integration recovered an aging-associated relationship between colonic methylation and cognition while identifying a largely distinct set of functionally coherent candidate genes. These findings complement supervised feature selection and provide candidates for investigating enteric neural involvement in cognitive aging, without establishing an age-independent association or a causal gut-to-brain mechanism.

From Data to Duty: An Informatics Blueprint for Pediatric Oncology Trials.
desc: [Pediatric blood & cancer] The data generated by cooperative-group clinical trials have transformed outcomes for children with cancer, yet the infrastructure underlying their collection and use has not kept pace with advances in informatics and data science. Data collection on pediatric oncology trials remains largely manual: Clinical research assistants abstract values from medical records and key them into electronic case report forms, a process that is costly, slow, inconsistent, and error-prone. Data are often siloed within trial networks for years after a study closes, limiting their value for secondary research, particularly for rare cancers. In this consensus blueprint, an interdisciplinary group of pediatric oncologists, clinical informaticians, data scientists, nurses, clinical research assistants, drug developers, and parent advocates outlines a pragmatic path forward across three components of the data lifecycle: collection, processing, and sharing. We argue that case report forms should be bound to standardized common data elements; that automated data abstraction from electronic health records, including via large language models with human-in-the-loop validation, should replace much of today's manual abstraction; that paper chemotherapy roadmaps should be reconceived as computable artifacts; and that clinical trials data should be deposited in publicly accessible repositories with appropriate governance as soon as practically feasible. We discuss facilitators and barriers within each component, including standards adoption, regulatory complexity, financial sustainability, and workforce capacity. We propose concrete actions for funders, clinical trials networks, professional societies, and industry. The technology to achieve these goals exists today, and widespread adoption requires coordinated leadership, sustainable funding models, and a cultural shift that recognizes data stewardship as an ethical imperative and a duty to the children and families we serve.

title: Breaking the Barrier of Hard Samples: A Data-Centric Approach to Synthetic Data for Medical Tasks
desc: Data scarcity and quality issues remain significant barriers to developing robust predictive models in medical research. Traditional reliance on real-world data often leads to biased models with poor generalizability across diverse patient populations. Synthetic data generation has emerged as a promising solution, yet challenges related to these samples' representativeness and effective utilization persist. This paper introduces Profile2Gen, a novel data-centric framework designed to guide the generation and refinement of synthetic data, focusing on addressing hard-to-learn samples in regression tasks. We conducted approximately 18,000 experiments to validate its effectiveness across six medical datasets, utilizing seven state-of-the-art generative models. Results demonstrate that refined synthetic samples can reduce predictive errors and enhance model reliability. Additionally, we generalize the DataIQ framework to support regression tasks, enabling its application in broader contexts. Statistical analyses confirm that our approach achieves equal or superior performance compared to models trained exclusively on real data.

desc: [Proceedings of the ... International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications. International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications] Conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs) have enabled high-fidelity computational staining and destaining of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) in digital pathology whole-slide images (WSI). However, their ability to generalize to out-of-distribution WSIs across institutions without retraining remains insufficiently characterized, limiting scalable clinical translation. Previously developed cGAN models trained on 102 registered prostate core biopsy WSIs from Brigham and Women's Hospital were evaluated on 82 spatially unregistered WSIs from three Stanford University patients. To mitigate domain shift without retraining, a preprocessing pipeline consisting of histogram-based stain normalization for H&E-stained WSIs and channel-wise intensity calibration for unstained WSIs was developed. Because image registration was intentionally omitted for real-world deployment conditions, the reported quantitative results are conservative lower bounds reflecting both model performance and limited spatial alignment. Under these conditions, virtual destaining achieved a Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) of 0.854, structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 0.699, and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 18.41 dB. H&E restaining from computationally destained outputs outperformed direct staining from ground-truth unstained inputs across all metrics (PCC: 0.798 vs. 0.715; SSIM: 0.756 vs. 0.718; PSNR: 20.08 vs. 18.51 dB), suggesting that preprocessing quality may be more limiting than model capacity. Qualitative pathological review indicated that benign glandular structures were more reliably preserved, and malignant glands were often rendered with vessel-like morphologies. These findings support the feasibility of applying cGAN-based computational H&E staining and destaining generative models to external WSI datasets using preprocessing-based adaptation alone, and identify malignant gland preservation for future domain adaptation.

title: FlowScope: 3D Scene Flow Pretraining Improves Surgical Robot Policies
desc: Imitation learning for surgical robots is limited by the cost of collecting demonstrations. Meanwhile, many robot-assisted procedures are recorded as stereo video, yet policies cannot learn from them directly; clinical video carries no action labels. We present FlowScope, which pretrains a surgical policy network on unlabeled clinical video by forecasting scene flow, the metric 3D motion of scene points, with labels computed by off-the-shelf stereo depth and optical flow models. We pretrain the trunk of an Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) on a dataset of 1,149 clinical procedures (1.35M clips) and discard the flow head afterward, so the deployed policy is a standard ACT with no added inference cost. On a real surgical robotic system, FlowScope raises needle pickup success from 54% to 90% and first-handover success on needle regrasp from 4% to 52% (full task: 2% to 14%) over training from scratch (n=50 trials each), and retains its gains with a generative flow-matching action head. Ablations indicate that metric 3D motion is the strongest pretraining signal among those tested; kinematics, 2D tracks, depth alone, and scale-free 3D flow, each paired with kinematics, yield smaller or no gains. Representation analyses suggest that scene-flow pretraining encodes metric needle depth more accurately, that kinematics pretraining increases reliance on the robot state, and that needle-depth probes follow the ordering of real-robot success where offline validation error does not.
